title: Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer
authors: Debarshi Kundu, Swaroop Ghosh, Vasant G Honavar
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) optimize circuit angles through repeated quantum-device evaluations, often facing vanishing gradients and high optimization costs. We ask whether a large language model (LLM) can write these angles directly. Extending *weight-space programming* from classical networks to quantum circuits, we provide a frontier LLM (\gpt) with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions. Its angles are executed exactly as written, without returning losses, gradients, or accuracy feedback. Across 139 requests, we test handwritten-digit classification, VQE ground-state estimation for spin chains and H$_2$, and MaxCut QAOA, comparing against random weights, classical optimization, and optimization initialized with LLM weights on the same circuit. When parameters have interpretable structure, the LLM matches or approaches the optimizer: it achieves 95--100\% of the energy spectrum on every VQE problem, derives the exact H$_2$ ground state in closed form, finds optimal depth-one QAOA angles for every graph, and reaches 93--96\% accuracy on digits 3 versus 8 with 12--18 hand-written weights, outperforming an optimizer trained on the same ten examples. Its weights are also strong warm starts: optimization reaches its best value after a median of one evaluation rather than hundreds. Allowed to design circuits, the LLM chooses data-dependent rotation chains encoding pixel importance in all 30 cases (one qubit for binary tasks, one chain per qubit for ten classes), reaching 65\% accuracy across ten digits. Yet the approach fails in opaque weight spaces: accuracy drops to chance when fixed circuits exceed 30 weights, while optimization improves. It is also sensitive to gate conventions: 6 of 42 QAOA replies reverse mixing-angle signs and fail. We release all prompts, replies, and scores.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM can directly write effective variational quantum circuit parameters without optimizer feedback when the parameter space has interpretable structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM-written parameters could reduce costly quantum-device optimization evaluations, either as direct solutions or as strong optimizer warm starts.
method: Provide the LLM with the problem, circuit, and gate conventions.

infographic.watch_item: Reliability depends on parameter interpretability and gate conventions: fixed circuits exceeding 30 weights fell to chance classification accuracy, and 6 of 42 QAOA replies used incorrect mixing-angle signs.
infographic.paper_title: Weight-Space Programming of Variational Quantum Circuits: Large Language Models Write Quantum Circuit Parameters Without an Optimizer

title: Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors
authors: Erik Connerty, Jonathan Eastridge, Taylor Patti, Gerasimos Angelatos, Ethan N. Evans
abstract: Simulating high dimensional unstructured Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with quantum processors is a major challenge with significant potential benefit. Existing methods have been demonstrated at small qubit counts, on simplifications of realistic problems. We implement a quantum reservoir network (QRN) for forecasting high-dimensional unstructured PDEs using up to 52 qubits on IBM superconducting hardware. Our method is gradient-free and does not suffer from the challenges of variational quantum algorithms. Instead, the QRN provides a large kernel space, up to 2^52 dimensions and beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, that remains useful under current hardware noise levels. Furthermore, a partial measure-and-reset mechanism enables total circuit runtime for ~24 times the qubit coherence time, so qubit lifetimes do not limit the forecast horizon. Thus, our method enables forecasting realistic unstructured nonlinear PDEs on quantum hardware. Typical difficulties associated with predicting large scale PDEs, such as transpilation, exponential shot requirements, hardware noise, and short qubit lifetimes are mitigated through careful design considerations and a dynamic observable reconstruction method. We validate our approach using a ~34k cell unstructured 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and a challenging nonlinear Gray--Scott reaction--diffusion problem, demonstrating high fidelity prediction on CUDA-Q simulation and on 26 and 52-qubit superconducting quantum processors. Specifically, we show that adding QRN features to an autoencoder linear prediction pipeline reduces prediction error by 21%-43%. Finally, we demonstrate closed-loop autoregressive PDE forecasting on these problems. This work demonstrates, for the first time, quantum circuits with depth beyond qubit lifetimes achieving accurate unstructured mesh forecasting on highly nonlinear PDEs.

infographic.key_insight: A quantum reservoir network enables nonlinear PDE forecasting on up to 52 superconducting qubits, with partial measure-and-reset supporting circuit runtimes about 24 times the qubit coherence time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach extends quantum-assisted forecasting to unstructured engineering meshes while mitigating hardware noise, transpilation overhead, measurement demands, and limited qubit lifetimes.
method: Encode PDE dynamics in a gradient-free quantum reservoir coupled to an autoencoder-based linear predictor.
Use partial measure-and-reset to sustain reservoir operation beyond individual qubit coherence times.
Apply dynamic observable reconstruction to mitigate measurement demands.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on approximately 34,000-cell 2D cylinder flow at Reynolds number 1000 and nonlinear Gray–Scott dynamics, using CUDA-Q simulation and 26- and 52-qubit hardware, showed 21%–43% lower prediction error when QRN features were added.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish end-to-end computational advantage over classical forecasting methods; measurement costs and hardware overhead remain important to assess.
infographic.paper_title: Realizing Unstructured PDE Forecasting on Superconducting Quantum Processors

title: Towards large-scale ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Efficient Sampling-based Quantum Computing Algorithms
authors: Ankit Khandelwal, Nirmal M R, Aaryav Mishra, Debasmita Bhoumik, Dhinakaran Vinayagamurthy, M Girish Chandra
abstract: Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) requires the calculation of highly accurate electronic-structure energies and nuclear forces at every time step, which can quickly become computationally expensive. Sample-based quantum diagonalization offers a route to such calculations on quantum hardware, but its use in AIMD simulations has so far been limited to active spaces of about 20 qubits. In these spaces, exact diagonalization is tractable, and the quantum circuits are typically built from standard coupled-cluster amplitudes. Here, we introduce SqDRIFT-AIMD, which combines randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT) with analytical nuclear gradients. With SqDRIFT-AIMD, we obtain more accurate ground-state energies than the conventional coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) driven AIMD simulation for the $40$-qubit active space. We apply SqDRIFT-AIMD to study the dynamics of proton transfer in the Zundel cation, using circuits executed on IBM Heron r3 quantum processors. SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the $40$-qubit double-well PES and stay within a few m$E_\text{h}$ of CCSD at 52 qubits. The $40$-qubit SqDRIFT-AIMD trajectory tracks the SHCI-driven proton transfer to within $1.33$ mÅ and exhibits excellent total energy conservation, with a standard deviation of only $0.245$ m$E_\text{h}$. These results extend quantum-centric AIMD to active spaces beyond the reach of exact diagonalization.

infographic.key_insight: SqDRIFT-AIMD combines sampling-based quantum diagonalization with analytical nuclear gradients to extend quantum-centric molecular dynamics beyond active spaces tractable by exact diagonalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a path toward accurate electronic energies and nuclear forces for larger molecular simulations using quantum hardware.
method: Use randomized sample-based Krylov quantum diagonalization (SqDRIFT).
Combine electronic-structure calculations with analytical nuclear gradients for AIMD.

infographic.evidence_signal: At 40 qubits, SqDRIFT energies fall below CCSD across the double-well potential, while its AIMD trajectory tracks SHCI-driven proton transfer within 1.33 mÅ and conserves total energy with a standard deviation of 0.245 mE_h; at 52 qubits, energies remain within a few mE_h of CCSD.

infographic.paper_title: Towards large-scale ab initio Molecular Dynamics Simulation with Efficient Sampling-based Quantum Computing Algorithms

title: Sign-hedged Beam QAOA:Scaling Quantum Optimization Algorithms
authors: Anupama Ray, Arush Sharma
abstract: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) encodes a combinatorial objective as an Ising Hamiltonian and alternates cost and mixer operations for p rounds. Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) scales further by using the resulting correlations, whether variables tend to agree or disagree, to eliminate variables one at a time. But each inferred sign is accepted irrevocably, so a single early mistake propagates through every later reduction and can discard the global optimum. As elimination proceeds, residuals shrink while effective edge density typically rises, so later decisions face denser Ising problems, a regime that fully connected Sherrington Kirkpatrick (SK) instances stress test directly. This paper proposes sign-hedged beam RQAOA, which retains the variable or pair selected by standard RQAOA, explores both possible sign assignments, keeps the best B residual problems according to a classical score, and completes each survivor with ordinary RQAOA. On frustrated SK instances, where standard recursion collapses to AR 0.474, beam recovers near-optimal AR 0.998 at the same p. We evaluate the workflow on 50+ instances from HamLib and QOBLIB, spanning 4 and 5 regular and Erdos Renyi MaxCut graphs, Sherrington Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glasses, and cardinality-constrained portfolio optimization, with up to 60 qubits and hardware runs on ibm kingston and ibm marrakesh. Matched simulator and device cells show consistent beam rankings: simulation and hardware agree that beam recovers near-optimal approximation ratio (AR) where standard recursion fails. These gains come from additional residual-circuit evaluations, classical pruning, and exact solution of a small core, rather than from increasing p, beam is a decision-side optimization atop fixed-p QAOA/RQAOA, not a claim that quantum circuits alone scale with qubit count.

infographic.key_insight: Sign-hedged beam RQAOA reduces irreversible elimination errors by exploring both sign assignments, recovering near-optimal solutions where standard recursion fails.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method improves fixed-depth QAOA/RQAOA through decision-side search rather than deeper quantum circuits, trading additional computation for better solution quality.
method: Keep standard RQAOA’s variable or pair selection, but branch on both possible signs.
Retain the best B residual problems using a classical score.
Complete survivors with ordinary RQAOA and solve a small core exactly.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 50+ benchmark instances up to 60 qubits, including runs on IBM Kingston and Marrakesh, the abstract reports consistent beam rankings; on frustrated SK instances, AR improves from 0.474 to 0.998 at unchanged circuit depth p.
infographic.watch_item: Gains require extra residual-circuit evaluations, classical pruning, and exact core solving; they do not establish that quantum circuits alone scale with problem size.
infographic.paper_title: Sign-hedged Beam QAOA:Scaling Quantum Optimization Algorithms

title: Sequential vs parallel Strategies for Sharing Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks
authors: Satyaki Manna, Arindam Mitra, Sumit Mukherjee
abstract: Information can be extracted from a quantum system in a sustainable manner, allowing the system to be reused for further information extraction through subsequent interactions. We investigate the possibility of consensus between two experimentally feasible methods, namely, parallel and sequential sharing, that enable multiple observers to extract information encoded in a quantum system. We show that any statistics generated by a parallel sharing strategy can be reproduced by a sequential strategy when only two observers are involved. However, when more than two observers participate in sharing quantum correlations, certain statistics achievable through parallel strategies cannot be reproduced by sequential strategies. Moreover, we demonstrate that sharing quantum advantage through a parallel strategy is impossible for a class of communication tasks involving two decoding measurements, thereby establishing an arbitrarily large gap between the sustainability of quantum advantage under sequential and parallel strategies. This naturally raises the question of whether this impossibility extends to communication tasks involving more than two decoding measurements. We show that, while parallel sharing of quantum advantage is impossible in a 3-bit random access code (RAC), it becomes possible in a 3-bit parity-oblivious RAC, where at most two observers can simultaneously obtain a quantum advantage by performing measurements on two imperfect clones of the initially prepared quantum system. Our findings have potential applications in the development of quantum communication networks and distributed quantum information processing.

infographic.key_insight: Sequential sharing reproduces all two-observer parallel statistics and can sustain quantum advantage for arbitrarily more observers in certain tasks, while parallel sharing becomes useful in specific constrained tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Quantum communication networks should choose sequential reuse or parallel distribution according to the task, since these architectures can support very different numbers of advantaged observers.
method: Compare statistics achievable through sequential and parallel information sharing.
Analyze quantum-advantage sharing in tasks with two decoding measurements.
Contrast parallel sharing in 3-bit random access codes (RACs) and parity-oblivious RACs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical results: two-observer statistical equivalence in one direction, an arbitrarily large sequential–parallel sustainability gap, and parallel advantage for at most two observers in a 3-bit parity-oblivious RAC using imperfect clones.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are task-dependent, and the abstract does not report experimental validation or robustness to implementation noise.
infographic.paper_title: Sequential vs parallel Strategies for Sharing Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks

title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays
authors: Zhihao Zhang, Shuaifan Cao, Xinyang Yu, Yanyan Chen, Yueyang Min, Yingzhou Li
abstract: Scalable quantum computation requires reconciling programmability with simple, high-fidelity control. Here, we propose a universal fault-tolerant architecture using globally driven dual-species atom arrays. In a hybrid neutral-atom system, interspecies Rydberg interactions enable qubit addressability without locally addressed quantum gates. We construct a universal native instruction set, Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL), and show that crosstalk errors can be suppressed to the $10^{-4}$ level. We compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, and parallelize the compilation to suppress crosstalk. Under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, we obtain an error-correction threshold of $1.43\%$ for the resulting quantum memory and a logical error rate below $10^{-9}$ for magic states cultivated at an experimentally accessible Rydberg Rabi frequency. By replacing local gate addressing with atom-mediated selectivity, this architecture removes the associated calibration requirements, offering a route to simpler control for large-scale fault-tolerant neutral-atom computation.

infographic.key_insight: Globally driven dual-species atom arrays could support universal fault-tolerant quantum computing without locally addressed quantum gates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Atom-mediated selectivity replaces local gate addressing, potentially simplifying control and reducing associated calibration requirements as neutral-atom processors scale.
method: Use interspecies Rydberg interactions to enable selective qubit operations under global driving.
Construct a universal native instruction set: Global Rydberg Atom Instruction Language (GRAIL).
Compile surface-code error correction and magic state cultivation into GRAIL, parallelizing operations to suppress crosstalk.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports crosstalk suppression to the 10^-4 level and, under a hardware-inferred circuit-level noise model, a 1.43% quantum-memory error-correction threshold and cultivated magic-state logical error below 10^-9.
infographic.watch_item: The reported performance is model-based; experimental validation must establish whether dual-species control and residual errors match the assumed noise model.
infographic.paper_title: A Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Architecture with Globally Driven Atom Arrays

title: Rotational Encoding of Objective Functions for Quantum Optimization
authors: Sonia Yang, Ali Al-Bayaty, Shanyan Chen, Marek Perkowski
abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Angular Rotational Counter (ARC), a novel approach to represent objective functions that can be decomposed as a weighted sum of Boolean functions. ARC encodes the objective as an accumulated sum of quantum rotations onto a single-qubit register instead of a multi-qubit register used in much of the previous literature. We mathematically establish and experimentally validate that these rotations sum to the objective value for all possible solutions and derive the relationship between the resulting measurement probabilities and the objective. This design was applied to construct a quantum oracle for the state assignment problem of finite automata and state machines using a weighted Hamming distance cost function, which is a special case of the quadratic assignment problem. We evaluate this oracle design on 26 benchmarks and compare it with corresponding Boolean-based oracles on four cost metrics. Across these benchmarks, the oracle with ARC produces a mean reduction in the qubit count of 20.8%, gate count of 89.3%, circuit depth of 92.4%, and quantum cost of 90.6%. These results demonstrate substantial reductions in circuit cost for the evaluated benchmarks and establish rotational encoding as a promising approach for representing objective functions in optimization based on quantum search algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: The Angular Rotational Counter (ARC) encodes a weighted sum of Boolean functions as accumulated rotations on one objective qubit rather than a multi-qubit objective register.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ARC can reduce quantum optimization oracle resources, potentially making quantum-search circuits more practical under qubit and circuit-depth constraints.
method: Translate weighted Boolean objective terms into accumulated single-qubit rotations.
Derive how measurement probabilities relate to the encoded objective value.
Build a state-assignment oracle using a weighted Hamming distance cost function.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 26 state-assignment benchmarks, ARC oracles averaged reductions of 20.8% in qubits, 89.3% in gates, 92.4% in circuit depth, and 90.6% in quantum cost versus corresponding Boolean-based oracles.
infographic.watch_item: These oracle resource savings do not establish end-to-end optimization speedups; rotation precision and measurement overhead need assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Rotational Encoding of Objective Functions for Quantum Optimization

title: Modular and Looping Quantum Photonic Processing Unit for Quantum Computing
authors: Denis Stanev, Nicolò Spagnolo, Fabio Sciarrino
abstract: Photonic processors are emerging as promising platforms in the race towards the realization of practical universal quantum computers. Several architectures with universal capabilities have been proposed for their implementation via a photonic platform, each with their own set of benefits and drawbacks. In this work we propose an architecture for a universal photonic quantum computer. The proposed architecture is modular, allowing for a high degree of flexibility and scalability, and relies on a loop-based structure, significantly reducing the number of physical components required to implement it experimentally. We prove that our architecture is universal, deterministic, and compatible with the quantum circuital model, as well as reprogrammable and capable of adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we showcase its functioning via numerical simulation on specific examples, by using machine learning techniques on a set of fundamental linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain some of the building blocks used in the architecture. The obtained results can be used to highlight the benefits and the drawbacks of the proposed architecture, as well as the route for future developments towards its physical implementation.

infographic.key_insight: A modular, loop-based photonic architecture is proposed for universal, deterministic quantum computing with fewer physical components.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reprogrammability, adaptive measurements, and compatibility with the quantum circuit model offer a flexible design path toward scalable photonic processors.
method: Use a modular, loop-based architecture to reduce physical component requirements.
Prove universality, determinism, and compatibility with the quantum circuit model.
Apply machine learning to linear and nonlinear optical components to obtain architectural building blocks.

infographic.watch_item: Practical feasibility remains to be established experimentally, particularly for repeated loop operations and the required nonlinear optical components.
infographic.paper_title: Modular and Looping Quantum Photonic Processing Unit for Quantum Computing

title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction for Bypassing Optimization Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
authors: Jamie Evander Ghozaly, Pekik Nurwantoro, Gagus Ketut Sunnardianto, Yanoar P. Sarwono, Leong-Chuan Kwek
abstract: The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) remains a cornerstone hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for quantum simulation, yet its scalability is fundamentally constrained by heavy measurement overheads. While strategies such as variance-preserved shot reduction (VPSR) mitigates this cost, they suffer from convergence instability and optimization stagnation caused by finite-sample bias in limited pilot shots. To overcome this limitation, we introduce delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR), an analytically enhanced shot allocation strategy that rigorously mitigates finite-sample instability. Utilizing the multivariate delta method, we derive explicit higher-order bias correction terms for the empirical reduction factor. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations reveal that incorporating higher-order statistical moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, provides the gradient resolution necessary to bypass noise-induced barren plateaus. DSCR significantly accelerates convergence compared to standard VPSR across diverse noise and resource regimes while matching or decreasing cumulative measurement costs, establishing a mathematically rigorous framework for variance-stabilized shot allocation on near-term hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Delta-corrected shot reduction (DCSR) corrects finite-sample bias in VQE measurement allocation to stabilize convergence and bypass noise-induced optimization plateaus.
infographic.engineering_relevance: DCSR could reduce measurement overhead in near-term quantum simulation while preserving the statistical resolution needed for reliable optimization.
method: Extend variance-preserved shot reduction with analytical finite-sample corrections.
Use the multivariate delta method to derive higher-order bias corrections to the empirical reduction factor.
Incorporate higher-order moments, including skewness and kurtosis, to improve shot allocation stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical analysis and numerical simulations showing faster convergence than standard VPSR across varied noise and resource regimes, with equal or lower cumulative measurement costs.
infographic.watch_item: Higher-order moment estimates may themselves be unstable with very few pilot shots; the abstract does not report hardware validation or quantitative gains.
infographic.paper_title: Delta-Corrected Shot Reduction for Bypassing Optimization Plateaus in Variational Quantum Eigensolvers

title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
authors: Nader Mostaan, Peter Schmelcher, Rick Mukherjee
abstract: We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

infographic.key_insight: A tunable XXZ interaction combined with single-qubit operations provides a unified route to arbitrary two-qubit gates in neutral-atom processors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Flexible native gate selection could reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead without requiring a separate interaction mechanism for each gate.
method: Propose a Rydberg-atom realization of XXZ coupling with tunable anisotropy.
Combine the interaction with optimally controlled global microwave pulses.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports implementations of these target gates but provides no numerical fidelities, noise benchmarks, or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental feasibility will depend on interaction tunability and pulse robustness under realistic neutral-atom noise.
infographic.paper_title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms

title: Rapid high-purity loading of barium ion via relayed selectivity from naturally abundant source
authors: Zichun Zhou, Xuhui Yao, Jiaze Li, Yuncheng Xie, Haozhe Shi, Yanxin Liu
abstract: Trapped ions is one of the promising platforms for realizing quantum information processing and quantum simulation. Selective and rapid loading of a specific isotope lays the critical foundation for such purpose particularly when scaling up the system size. Here we demonstrate a new method for rapid isotope-selective loading of $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ or $^{135}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$, two types of promising ion qubits, from naturally abundant source using a three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme. Neutral atoms are selected on the narrow 791 nm $6s^2\,{}^1S_0\rightarrow6s6p\,{}^3P_1^o$ transition, resonantly transferred at 554 nm to $6s6d\,{}^3D_1$, and ionized using an existing 532 nm Raman beam. A spectral-overlap analysis based on isotope and hyperfine shifts shows relayed selectivity that the second step can further suppress undesired-isotope excitation and no contaminant ion is detected during our entire experiment. Besides, the resonant drive of the second step excitation yields a prominent loading rate of the selected species. This strategy using multi-step excitations to establish relayed selectivity can be extended to high-purity loading of other species of ions.

infographic.key_insight: A three-step, ultraviolet-free photoionization scheme rapidly loads selected barium isotopes from a naturally abundant source, with successive resonant transitions reinforcing isotope selectivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Rapid, high-purity loading of ¹³⁷Ba⁺ or ¹³⁵Ba⁺ could support scaling trapped-ion quantum computing and simulation systems.
method: Select neutral isotopes using the narrow 791 nm transition.
Resonantly transfer atoms at 554 nm, further suppressing unwanted isotopes.
Ionize using an existing 532 nm Raman beam.
infographic.evidence_signal: Spectral-overlap analysis supports relayed selectivity, and the authors report rapid loading with no contaminant ions detected throughout the experiment.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract gives no numerical loading rates or contamination detection limits, limiting quantitative performance assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Rapid high-purity loading of barium ion via relayed selectivity from naturally abundant source

title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
authors: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser
abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.55x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents discovered formally verified quantum programs with reported improvements of up to 290× over prior baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Proof-guided algorithm discovery could reduce quantum resource requirements for scientific applications before hardware can directly test the programs.
method: Encode quantum programs and formal problem specifications in Lean.
Use Gemini 4 agents to synthesize programs and verify correctness and cost.
Coordinate agent teams through shared wikis and organized conferences.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over prior baselines of up to 2.55× for parallel search, 290× for quantum arithmetic, and 11×, 8× and 2.5× for simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug metabolism, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Formal correctness and cost guarantees depend on the encoded specifications and cost models; these gains do not by themselves establish performance on physical quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI

title: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination
authors: A. Duplinskiy, M. J. Filipovich, A. I. Lvovsky
abstract: Almost all solutions to vision tasks $\unicode{x2014}$ offered by nature and technology alike $\unicode{x2014}$ rely on capturing an image using a lens or a similar optical instrument, followed by computational analysis by neurons of a brain or a digital computer. This approach is inherently suboptimal in photon-limited and noisy conditions, where critical information is irreversibly lost at the measurement stage. We address this gap by introducing AI-driven optimization of quantum measurements on the incoming photons, learning how to extract the maximum possible information for a given computer vision task from each incoming photon. The trained measurement consists of a diffractive optical neural network (DONN) followed by a detector array. We train the DONN with a quantum information-theoretic objective that maximizes the rate at which the discrimination error decays as photons accumulate. The resulting measurement achieves exponentially lower error than both direct imaging and a DONN optimized for single-photon discrimination. We validate the advantage in a noiseless setting as well as a photon-counting experiment with an electron-multiplying CCD with the noise corresponding to $10^4$ photons per single signal photon, where the measurement also learns to mitigate the detector noise.

infographic.key_insight: AI-optimized quantum measurements extract task-relevant information before photodetection, achieving exponentially lower discrimination error as photons accumulate than direct imaging or single-photon-optimized measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Task-specific optical measurement design could improve photon-efficient machine vision in low-light and noisy sensing systems.
method: Train a diffractive optical neural network followed by a detector array.
Use a quantum information-theoretic objective to maximize the discrimination-error decay rate as photons accumulate.
Optimize the measurement to mitigate detector noise.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation in a noiseless setting and a photon-counting experiment using an electron-multiplying CCD, with noise corresponding to 10^4 photons per signal photon.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish how well task-specific measurements generalize to new visual tasks or changing noise conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Experimental visual quantum state discrimination

title: Evaluation of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Network Anomaly Detection
authors: Swathi Chandrasekhar, Shiva Raj Pokhrel
abstract: The proliferation of Internet-connected devices has intensified the risk of large-scale network intrusions, necessitating more advanced detection methodologies for the post quantum era. This work presents, to the best of our knowledge, a com- prehensive investigation of quantum machine learning (QML) for anomaly detection on the BoT-IoT dataset, a widely adopted benchmark for IoT security. Leveraging feature-engineered rep- resentations, we implement and evaluate four representative quantum classifiers: Quantum Support Vector Classification (QSVC), Quantum Neural Networks (QNN), and Variational Quantum Classifiers (VQC).

infographic.key_insight: The study evaluates quantum machine learning classifiers for IoT network anomaly detection without reporting performance outcomes in the abstract.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work explores QML-based intrusion detection for connected-device networks, though practical advantages over classical methods remain unestablished.
method: Use feature-engineered representations of network traffic.
Implement quantum classifiers, including QSVC, QNN, and VQC.
Evaluate anomaly detection on the BoT-IoT benchmark.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract identifies BoT-IoT as the evaluation dataset but provides no metrics, classical baselines, or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract claims four classifiers but names only three, leaving the full model comparison unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluation of Quantum Machine Learning Models for Network Anomaly Detection

title: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing
authors: Jean Senellart, Benjamin Stott, Stephen Wein, Esperanza Cuenca Gomez, Pascale Senellart, Shane Mansfield
abstract: Estimates of when photonic devices outgrow classical simulation are hard to compare: even for single-photon boson sampling, quoted thresholds range from 50 to 98 photons, as they rest on different tasks and assumptions. We propose as a common unit the time a classical computer needs to draw one sample from the device's exact output distribution, up to floating-point rounding. Only exactness applies equally to every kind of light, since the cost of approximate sampling depends on the accuracy required. The simulability frontier is the device size at which our fastest exact sampler produces one sample per second on a fixed machine; this device size increases with better hardware and algorithms. As the time per sample grows exponentially with the number of detected photons, doubling the machine speed moves the frontier by about one photon, whereas a better algorithm changes the growth rate. We measure the frontier with photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library of exact samplers for single photons, entangled photons from quantum emitters, vacuum-single-photon superpositions and squeezed light. Each sampler is validated against a simulator sharing no code with it. On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5. For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.

infographic.key_insight: A common benchmark—one exact sample per second—makes photonic simulation limits comparable and shows that source coherence can increase classical simulation cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware speedups shift the simulability frontier modestly, while algorithms that reduce exponential scaling can have a larger impact.
method: Define the frontier using exact output sampling, up to floating-point rounding, on fixed hardware.
Benchmark photonic-engines GPU samplers across single-photon, entangled, coherent-superposition and squeezed-light inputs.
Validate each sampler against an independent simulator sharing no code.
infographic.evidence_signal: On one NVIDIA H100, the frontier was 38.3 single photons and 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter; a fitted timing model estimated 41.5 squeezed inputs with mean photon number 0.5.
infographic.watch_item: These exact-sampling frontiers depend on the chosen hardware, algorithms and optical configuration; they do not establish limits for approximate classical sampling.
infographic.paper_title: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing

title: Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications
authors: Lúcio S. Fassarella
abstract: We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the \emph{Choi-Kraus operator-sum representation} and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems. We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup. This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references. The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.

infographic.key_insight: A unified quantum-channel framework supports mixed-state preparation, POVM measurements, and first-order simulation of Markovian dynamics without Trotterization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach provides a common mathematical foundation for implementing state preparation, generalized measurements, and open-system dynamics on digital quantum computers.
method: Represent quantum channels using Choi–Kraus operators and Stinespring dilation.
Recover mixed-state purification and Naimark dilation for POVMs.
Use a residual operator derived from the Liouvillian to construct an Euler-like, first-order dynamical channel.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical proofs and explicit examples implemented with Qiskit's AerSimulator, with code on GitHub, but gives no quantitative performance benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The dynamical approximation is only first order, so accuracy over repeated simulation steps requires attention to step size and accumulated error.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications

title: An efficient classical algorithm for OTOCs in chaotic quantum dynamics
authors: Yunchao Liu, Yihui Quek, Shreya Vardhan, Tianci Zhou
abstract: Estimating out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in individual instances of random quantum circuits has been proposed as a candidate for verifiable quantum advantage, and demonstrated to be hard for conventional classical algorithms such as tensor networks and Monte Carlo. Using insights from quantum chaos, we develop and implement a polynomial-time classical algorithm for the four-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and the eight-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in typical instances of one-dimensional (1D) quantum circuits. Our results demonstrate average-case classical tractability of estimating OTOCs in the sensitive regime where circuit-to-circuit fluctuations are large. Our algorithm organizes the OTOC into a rapidly converging series, where the leading term includes contributions from histories within permutation degrees of freedom in the replicated Hilbert space, and subleading terms arise from excursions outside this space. Although chaos is often viewed as an insurmountable barrier to classical simulation, our algorithm exploits a form of dephasing caused by chaos, which suppresses the subleading terms. We provide strong theoretical and numerical evidence to support this suppression. Further, we demonstrate that practical implementations of our algorithm estimate ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in 1D circuits with high accuracy, achieving higher signal-to-noise ratio at larger circuit depths compared to recent 2D experiments by Google. Extending our algorithm to higher dimensions, and resolving the status of quantum advantage in 2D OTOCs, remain open problems.

infographic.key_insight: Chaos-induced dephasing enables polynomial-time classical estimation of four- and eight-point OTOCs in typical 1D random quantum circuits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The algorithm provides a classical benchmark for OTOC-based quantum advantage claims in 1D chaotic circuits.
method: Expand each OTOC into a rapidly converging series in replicated Hilbert space.
Compute leading contributions from histories within permutation degrees of freedom.
Exploit chaos-induced dephasing to suppress corrections from excursions outside that space.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theoretical and numerical evidence supports correction suppression, while implementations achieve high accuracy in 1D and higher signal-to-noise at larger depths than recent Google 2D experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Extension to higher dimensions remains open, so the results do not resolve quantum advantage for 2D OTOCs.
infographic.paper_title: An efficient classical algorithm for OTOCs in chaotic quantum dynamics

title: GARI++: A General-Purpose Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Arshpreet Singh Maan, Francisco Garcia-Herrero, Daniel Bascones, Valentin Savin, Alexandru Paler
abstract: We present GARI++, a two-stage decoding pipeline achieving accuracy competitive with the state of the art across surface, bivariate bicycle and color codes without relying on ensembles. The first stage uses GARI, a normalized min-sum decoder with random serial scheduling on the GARI transformed matrix. The second stage decoder is used only for the cases that the first stage does not converge, and the decoder is configurable based on the choice of the QEC code. The first stage pipelines towards the second stage both the residual syndrome and the soft information. GARI++ pipelining is predictive, meaning that GARI++ chooses the first stage iteration outputs which are expected to deliver the best accuracy in the second stage. GARI++ motivates a hybrid FPGA-CPU architecture for real-time decoding. For example, under uniform circuit-level depolarising noise with a physical error rate of 0.001, the FPGA implementation of GARI achieves average latencies per round ranging from $201 ns$ to $11.8μs$ for surface code distances between 7 and 25. At the same time, due to the very low weight residuals output by the first stage, the average residual decoding time per round remains near constant and below one microsecond on a single Apple M2 core for surface code distances even up to 51 when using Union-Find and accuracy on par with correlated MWPM.

infographic.key_insight: GARI++ combines fast first-stage decoding with selective residual decoding to achieve accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods across several quantum error-correcting code families without ensembles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline motivates hybrid FPGA–CPU decoding, pairing hardware-accelerated GARI with CPU processing of low-weight residual errors.
method: Run GARI normalized min-sum decoding with random serial scheduling on the GARI-transformed matrix.
Invoke a code-configurable second-stage decoder only when GARI does not converge, forwarding residual syndrome and soft information.
Predictively select first-stage iteration outputs expected to yield the best second-stage accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: At circuit-level depolarising error rate 0.001, reported FPGA GARI average latency per round spans 201 ns–11.8 µs for surface-code distances 7–25; single-core Apple M2 Union-Find residual decoding averages below 1 µs through distance 51, with accuracy on par with correlated MWPM.
infographic.watch_item: Reported component averages do not establish worst-case end-to-end latency, including FPGA–CPU communication and second-stage workload bursts.
infographic.paper_title: GARI++: A General-Purpose Decoder for Quantum Error Correction

title: Long-distance quantum secure direct communication with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubits
authors: Meng-Dong Zhu, Jia-Wei Ying, Qi Zhang, Shi-Pu Gu, Xing-Fu Wang, Lan Zhou
abstract: The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code possesses a lattice periodic structure that enables the effective correction of small displacement errors induced by noise in phase space, which is indispensable for quantum computation. The GKP code was also used to construct a long-distance entanglement channel in quantum repeaters and distribute random keys in quantum key distribution (QKD). Using GKP encoding, we propose a quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) protocol that not only transmits the secret message directly, but also helps protect the safety of communication personnel. The exponential attenuation loss of photons can be overcome by the third-generation quantum repeater. Numerical simulation results demonstrate that secure transmission distance exceeding 1000 km is achievable with a 23 dB squeezing level. Furthermore, we establish a cost-based optimization framework to characterize the trade-off among secure communication distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources, enabling optimized repeater deployment and providing a systematic design strategy for scalable quantum repeater architectures. The results demonstrate the potential of combining GKP error correction for long-distance QSDC and quantum networks.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed GKP-encoded quantum secure direct communication protocol could transmit secret messages over more than 1000 km using third-generation quantum repeaters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cost-based optimization links secure distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources to guide scalable quantum network deployment.
method: Encode quantum information in GKP qubits to correct small phase-space displacement errors.
Use third-generation quantum repeaters to counter distance-dependent photon loss.
Optimize repeater deployment by balancing communication performance and resource cost.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations indicate secure transmission beyond 1000 km at a 23 dB squeezing level; the abstract reports no experimental demonstration.
infographic.watch_item: Practical feasibility depends on achieving 23 dB GKP squeezing and implementing reliable repeater operations at scale.
infographic.paper_title: Long-distance quantum secure direct communication with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubits

title: Initialization masks overcome decoding obstructions in compressed QAOA
authors: Emilio Semre, Steven Frankel
abstract: In compressed quantum optimization, a variational state is converted into a classical assignment by decoding noncommuting observables. We show that this step creates structural restrictions that changing the initialization can remove, even when increasing circuit depth cannot. For an explicit infinite family of connected cubic graphs on $n=3r$ vertices, with a fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder, every all-plus QAOA circuit has cut at most $2r$, at every finite depth and every real angle sequence. A uniform signed product-state mask at fixed depth-one angles has expected cut $13r/4$, an additive advantage $5n/12$; an infinite subfamily admits an optimal mask. A second construction retains a linear depth-one separation under weak weighted couplings, a bounded cost-angle domain and a specified production-encoder ordering. Noiseless simulations then test classical mask selection before energy optimization. On 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, one selected mask achieves mean ratio $0.9100$, versus $0.7067$ for the all-plus $X$ baseline and $0.9125$ for the best of $r^2$ separately optimized random masks. On complete cohorts of weighted MaxCut, sparse Ising, Max-2-XOR and Max-2-SAT, the selected mask also improves on the baseline at every size, but it trails the pool at small sizes and leads it significantly only at the larger MaxCut and Ising sizes. Finite-pool order statistics separate the effect of selection from that of drawing a random mask. The results distinguish decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance; they do not establish a quantum computational advantage.

infographic.key_insight: Changing initialization masks can overcome decoding restrictions in compressed QAOA that persist at every finite circuit depth with all-plus initialization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Classical mask selection offers a way to improve decoded solutions without increasing quantum circuit depth.
method: Prove an all-depth decoding obstruction for a fixed Pauli encoding on an infinite family of connected cubic graphs.
Show that random signed product-state masks yield a linear expected cut advantage at fixed depth-one angles.
Test classical mask selection before energy optimization using noiseless simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, one selected mask achieved a mean ratio of 0.9100, versus 0.7067 for the all-plus X baseline and 0.9125 for the best of r² separately optimized random masks.
infographic.watch_item: The simulations are noiseless, selected masks do not consistently beat the random-mask pool, and no quantum computational advantage is established.
infographic.paper_title: Initialization masks overcome decoding obstructions in compressed QAOA
